title: Chapter 124 — The Needle
paragraphs: The next morning the sea, not yet calmed, rolled in long, slow swells of enormous bulk, and, surging along in the Pequod's gurgling wake, pushed her forward like the outspread palms of giants. The strong, steady breeze blew so abundantly that sky and air seemed like vast billowing sails; the whole world boomed along before the wind. Muffled in the full morning light, the sun could not be seen, and was known only by the spread-out intensity of the place where he stood, where his bayonet rays moved forward in stacks. Heraldic splendors, as of crowned Babylonian kings and queens, reigned over everything. The sea was like a crucible of molten gold, bubbling and leaping with light and heat.

Keeping a spellbound silence for a long time, Ahab stood apart. Every time the teetering ship dipped her bowsprit low, he turned to look at the bright rays of the sun stretching out ahead; and when she sank deep by the stern, he turned around and saw where the sun stood behind them, and how the same yellow rays were blending with his unswerving wake.

"Ha, ha, my ship! You might well be taken now for the sea-chariot of the sun. Ho, ho! All you nations before my prow, I bring the sun to you! Yoke on the further billows; hallo! A tandem, I drive the sea!"
But, suddenly pulled up short by some contrary thought, he hurried to the helm and asked hoarsely which way the ship was heading.
"East-southeast, sir," said the frightened steersman.
"You lie!" striking him with his clenched fist. "Heading east at this hour in the morning, and the sun astern?"
At this everyone was dumbfounded; for somehow the phenomenon Ahab had just noticed had escaped everyone else — though its very glaring obviousness must have been the reason.

Thrusting his head halfway into the binnacle, Ahab caught one glimpse of the compasses; his uplifted arm slowly fell; for a moment he almost seemed to stagger. Standing behind him, Starbuck looked, and — behold! — the two compasses pointed east, and the Pequod was just as unerringly going west.

But before the first wild alarm could get abroad among the crew, the old man with a rigid laugh exclaimed: "I have it! It has happened before. Mr. Starbuck, last night's thunder turned our compasses — that's all. You've heard of such a thing before now, I take it."
"Aye; but it has never happened to me before, sir," said the pale mate gloomily.

Here it must be said that accidents like this have occurred in more than one case to ships in violent storms. The magnetic energy, as developed in the mariner's needle, is, as everyone knows, essentially one with the electricity seen in the heavens; so it is not much to be wondered at that such things should happen. In instances where the lightning has actually struck the vessel, so as to knock down some of the spars and rigging, the effect on the needle has at times been still more fatal: all its loadstone power has been destroyed, so that the formerly magnetic steel was of no more use than an old wife's knitting needle. But in either case, the needle never again recovers by itself the original power thus marred or lost; and if the binnacle compasses are affected, the same fate reaches all the others that may be in the ship, even if the lowest one were set into the kelson, the timber running along the keel inside the hold.

Standing deliberately in front of the binnacle and eyeing the turned-around compasses, the old man now took the exact bearing of the sun with the edge of his outstretched hand. Satisfied that the needles were exactly reversed, he shouted orders for the ship's course to be changed to match. The yards were put hard up, and once again the Pequod drove her undaunted bows into the opposing wind, for the supposedly fair one had only been fooling her.

Meanwhile, whatever his own secret thoughts were, Starbuck said nothing, but quietly issued all the necessary orders; while Stubb and Flask — who in some small degree seemed then to be sharing his feelings — likewise went along without a murmur. As for the men, though some of them rumbled low, their fear of Ahab was greater than their fear of Fate. But as ever before, the pagan harpooners remained almost wholly unimpressed; or if impressed, it was only with a certain magnetism shot into their kindred hearts from inflexible Ahab's.

For a while the old man paced the deck, lost in rolling daydreams. But happening to slip with his ivory heel, he caught sight of the crushed copper sight-tubes of the quadrant he had smashed on the deck the day before.

"You poor, proud heaven-gazer and sun's pilot! Yesterday I wrecked you, and today the compasses would gladly have wrecked me. So, so. But Ahab is lord over the level loadstone yet. Mr. Starbuck — a lance without a pole; a top-maul, and the smallest of the sail-maker's needles. Quick!"

Contributing, perhaps, to the impulse behind what he was now about to do were certain prudent motives, whose object might have been to revive the spirits of his crew by a stroke of his subtle skill, in a matter so wondrous as that of the inverted compasses. Besides, the old man well knew that to steer by reversed needles, though clumsily workable, was not a thing superstitious sailors would let pass without some shuddering and forebodings of evil.

"Men," he said, turning steadily to face the crew as the mate handed him the things he had asked for, "my men, the thunder has turned old Ahab's needles; but from this bit of steel Ahab can make one of his own that will point as true as any."
As he said this, the sailors exchanged shamefaced glances of slavish wonder, and waited with fascinated eyes for whatever magic might come next. But Starbuck looked away.

With a blow from the top-maul Ahab knocked off the steel head of the lance, and then, handing the mate the long iron rod that remained, told him to hold it upright without letting it touch the deck. Then, after repeatedly striking the upper end of this iron rod with the maul, he placed the blunted needle endwise on top of it and hammered that, less strongly, several times, the mate still holding the rod as before. Then, going through some small strange motions with it — whether necessary to the magnetizing of the steel, or merely meant to increase the awe of the crew, is uncertain — he called for linen thread; and moving to the binnacle, he slipped out the two reversed needles there and hung the sail-needle horizontally by its middle over one of the compass-cards. At first the steel went round and round, quivering and vibrating at either end; but at last it settled into its place, and Ahab, who had been intently watching for this result, stepped openly back from the binnacle and, pointing his outstretched arm toward it, exclaimed: "Look for yourselves, and see if Ahab is not lord of the level loadstone! The sun is east, and that compass swears it!"
One after another they peered in — for only their own eyes could convince men as ignorant as they were — and one after another they crept away.
Then you could see Ahab in all his fatal pride, in those fiery eyes full of scorn and triumph.
